name: Yusuf Lopez

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Yusuf. I'm a researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you tell me is confidential, and nothing goes back to your company with your name on it. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I run the payroll team at the head office of a hotel group, about sixty hotels. Seven of us pay around nine thousand staff, cleaners, chefs, receptionists, every two weeks. My day is checking timesheets that the hotels send in late, fixing overtime mistakes, and answering calls from a housekeeper in some seaside hotel who's been paid twenty pounds short.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like that it matters. If we get it wrong, somebody can't pay their rent, so I take it seriously. What wears me out is being new as a manager, I was promoted in March and two of my team are older than my dad, and the payroll system crashes every other Thursday right before the run.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the five pictures. The first one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, people should do real work and the computers can stay in their place. I don't post online much. At work I'd say it quietly to the older ones, who'd agree.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me nothing changes on the AI side, which suits me. But I'm getting married next summer to Amira, and between the wedding and the rent, money is tight even with savings. The hotels are always talking about cutting head office costs, so I never feel completely safe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going, learn the payroll system properly so I stop calling IT, and keep saving for the wedding, about 350 a month. I'd say no to any extra spending until after the wedding.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Not because of AI, because of money and getting married.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the wedding cost look like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Amira's family wants a proper wedding, two hundred guests, and my family does too, if I'm honest. My fiancée Amira and I have four months of savings, and the wedding alone would eat most of it. We'd manage, with family help.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you turn to if money got tight?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My father first, he runs a tiling business and he's always said there's work there. And the community at the mosque, people help each other. I'd never go to the government first, that's for people with no one.

I'd say it **quietly** to the older ones at work, who'd agree.
think: AI doesn't change things, but **wedding and rent** keep money tight.
Hotels always talk about **cutting head office**, so I never feel completely safe.
do: Learn the **payroll system** properly so I stop calling IT.
Save about **350 a month** for the wedding.
Say no to **extra spending** until after the wedding.
feel: **Uneasy** about money and the wedding, not about AI.
S0.quote: My fiancée Amira and I have four months of savings, and the wedding alone would eat most of it.
fieldNote: His pressure is the **wedding** and rent, independent of AI.
He looks to **family and community** first, not government.
He takes pride in **paying people correctly**.

steps.text: Learn the payroll system well enough to stop calling IT
Save 350 a month for the wedding next summer
Put off new purchases until after the wedding

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a shame, companies forgetting that people need work, not just profits. I'd say it to my father and at the mosque. At work I'd keep quiet and do my job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Payroll is checking, and checking is on the list. If a system checks timesheets and pays nine thousand people with two humans watching, my team of seven goes, and they don't need me. I've never touched these AI tools, so I'm not the obvious one to keep.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask my father seriously about joining the tiling business, maybe weekends first. I'd make the wedding smaller, or push it back a year. I'd keep saving and not spend on anything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I'm a person who likes things to stay the same, and this is everything changing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you learn the AI tools to keep your job?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe, if they made me, but I don't trust them with people's pay. A machine that pays a cleaner twenty pounds short won't pick up the phone and say sorry. I'd rather do something I understand.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would Amira agree to a smaller wedding?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She'd understand, but her mother wouldn't. We'd have a hard conversation. In the end I think we'd do the ceremony and a smaller meal, and save the big party for later.

do: Ask my father about joining **his tiling business** on weekends.

feel: **Anxious**, because he likes things the same and **everything changes**.
S1.quote: A machine that pays a cleaner twenty pounds short won't pick up the phone and say sorry.
fieldNote: He distrusts AI with **people's pay**, rooted in his care for staff.

The **wedding** is the first thing he would change.

steps.text: Work weekends in his father's tiling business
Hold a smaller wedding ceremony and meal
Keep saving 350 a month with no extra spending

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's dangerous and nobody voted for it. I'd say it at home and at the mosque. I wouldn't post anything, because what's the point.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think my job is gone in the first year. Payroll is all thinking work, and if a machine can do it better, the hotels will take it. Tiling is hands-on, so I'd have until about 2031, three years, and my father's business would need to keep going.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd leave payroll and go full-time with my father within a year. I'd postpone the wedding, or do it very small, and move in with my parents to save rent. I'd keep the savings for emergencies.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I don't like change, and this is all at once.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you feel about moving back with your parents?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Embarrassed, but practical. I'd be twenty-eight, engaged and back in my old bedroom, which isn't how I pictured married life. Amira would move in too, probably.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said nobody voted for it. Would you vote differently?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe, for whoever promised to slow it down. I'd still want people working, not getting handouts. But I'd want someone to stand up for ordinary workers.

I'd say it at home and **at the mosque**, not online.
think: My **payroll job goes** in the first year, because it's all thinking work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's still too fast for most people and we should slow it down. I'd say it to anyone who asked. At work I'd keep quiet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years means I keep payroll for maybe three or four years. That gets me through the wedding at least. But I'd be thirty-two with no job unless I learn tiling properly before 2031.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd get married next summer as planned, but smaller. I'd start working weekends with my father to learn the trade. I'd save every month and not buy a house.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed still. Five years isn't long when you hate change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why not buy a house?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because a mortgage on a payroll salary is a trap if the job goes. I'd rather rent for five years than owe the bank for a house I can't pay for in 2031. My father bought late, and he was fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell the older people on your team?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: To start thinking now. One of them, Doreen, is sixty-one and might just retire. The other, Kwame, is fifty-five and has a mortgage. I'd worry about him.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough time, so people should stop complaining and plan. I'd say it at the mosque. At work I'd be calm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With ten years I could stay in payroll most of my thirties and learn tiling slowly. Robots for tiling come around 2039, so I'd have a good run. I'd be about forty by then, and maybe I'd run my father's business.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd get married next summer and maybe have children. I'd keep payroll but learn tiling on weekends. I'd save for a house.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but I can sleep. It's far enough away.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you take over your father's business?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's the plan, if he lets me. My father has tiled bathrooms for thirty years, and I'd rather inherit his van than wait for a payroll robot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What about children? Does this change anything?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd still have them. But I'd want them to learn a trade as well as school. Hands and head, both.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because I'd lose payroll before I could learn tiling, and right in the middle of getting married. What would help is my family, honestly, and a company that gives proper notice and doesn't throw people out.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe about who gets paid right when machines do payroll. A housekeeper who gets paid twenty pounds short needs a person to call, and I've been that person for five years.

headlineQuote: A housekeeper who gets paid twenty pounds short needs a person to call, and I've been that person for five years.
portrait: Yusuf is a **27-year-old payroll manager** of seven at a hotel group's head office.
He **never uses AI**, dislikes change, and is engaged with a wedding planned next summer.
He looks to **family and his mosque** for support, and wants work over handouts.
He sees payroll as **checking work** that AI takes, so his fallback is his father's tiling business.
He is **uneasy** even in the plateau, and alarmed in the faster AGI pictures.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because he'd lose payroll before learning tiling and mid-wedding.
